title: The Dow Just Hit a Record High While AI Stocks Crashed. If Your Portfolio Is Tech-Heavy, Read This.
excerpt: Wall Street's sharpest sector rotation in months sent banks and healthcare soaring while Broadcom lost 13 per cent in a day. For NRI investors concentrated in Silicon Valley names, the message is uncomfortable but clear.
body:
On Thursday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 900 points to close at 51,561.93, a fresh all-time record. The S&P 500 rose 0.4 per cent. The Nasdaq Composite, the index most closely associated with technology and AI stocks, finished the day in the red. This is not a contradiction. It is a rotation, and for NRI investors whose portfolios are heavily weighted toward the technology sector, it is a signal worth understanding.

The catalyst was Broadcom. The semiconductor company reported quarterly earnings that by most measures were strong: revenue grew, AI-related sales continued to surge, and the company reiterated its full-year guidance. But the market had priced in perfection, and anything less than an upward revision to guidance was punished. Broadcom shares fell 13 per cent in a single session. The selloff rippled across the semiconductor sector. Micron Technology dropped nearly 8 per cent. ARM Holdings fell over 6 per cent. AMD declined 3.6 per cent.

## Where the Money Went

Rather than heading for the exits, investors moved capital from one sector to another. Goldman Sachs rose nearly 5 per cent. JPMorgan Chase climbed. UnitedHealth surged. American Express gained 4.6 per cent. Medtronic rose over 5 per cent. Blackstone advanced. The pattern was unmistakable: money was leaving richly valued AI and semiconductor stocks and flowing into financials, healthcare, and industrials — sectors that trade at lower valuations and offer more predictable earnings.

Patrick O'Hare of Briefing.com described it plainly: "The divergence in stock performance reflects a rotation of capital from leading tech names into traditional blue-chip stocks with lower beta." Market participants broadly characterised the move as a healthy correction that cools overheating in one segment without undermining the broader bull market.

## Why NRI Investors Are Disproportionately Exposed

This rotation carries particular significance for the Indian diaspora in the United States. A large proportion of NRIs work in the technology sector, and their financial portfolios reflect that concentration. Employee stock options, restricted stock units, and 401(k) allocations tend to be heavily weighted toward the companies they work for and the sector they know best.

The result is a double exposure. If you work at a semiconductor company and your savings are in semiconductor stocks, a sector rotation does not just affect your portfolio. It affects your compensation, your net worth, and your sense of financial security simultaneously. The standard advice to diversify is easy to give and hard to follow when your employer pays you in the very equity you should theoretically be selling.

The numbers illustrate the risk. Broadcom, which was trading above $479 before earnings, closed at $418.91. An NRI engineer holding 500 shares of Broadcom through an RSU plan lost roughly $30,000 in paper value in a single trading session. Multiply that pattern across Micron, AMD, and ARM, and the aggregate impact on diaspora wealth in Silicon Valley is substantial.

## What the Rotation Signals

Sector rotations are not inherently bearish. They can signal a maturing bull market where investors broaden their bets rather than concentrate in a single theme. The AI trade has been the dominant narrative in markets for over two years. Companies with any connection to artificial intelligence — chip designers, cloud providers, data centre builders — have been rewarded with premium valuations. That premium is now being tested.

The question is not whether AI will continue to grow. It will. The question is whether the stocks priced at 40 to 60 times earnings have already absorbed that growth. When Broadcom delivers strong results and the stock falls 13 per cent, the market is signalling that the price already reflected the good news. Any pause in the pace of improvement, any hint that the trajectory is merely excellent rather than extraordinary, becomes a selling trigger.

For NRI investors, the practical implication is straightforward: concentration is risk. A portfolio that is 60 or 70 per cent technology and semiconductor stocks has delivered exceptional returns over the past two years. It has also become a highly leveraged bet on a single narrative. Days like Thursday are a reminder that narratives shift faster than fundamentals do.

## What To Do With This Information

This is not a call to sell technology stocks and buy banks. It is a call to examine your actual portfolio composition, count the exposure you have through RSUs and options, and ask whether you would choose this allocation if you were starting from zero. If the answer is no, the rotation is offering you a window to rebalance into a mix that includes sectors now attracting capital: financials, healthcare, industrials, and dividend-paying blue chips.

The Dow's record high is not the story. The fact that it reached that record while the Nasdaq fell is. The market is telling you something about where value is moving. Whether you listen is a portfolio decision. Whether you act on it is a career one.

**Sources:** New York Post (June 2026); MarketWatch (June 2026); Barron's (June 2026); Briefing.com; BigGo Finance
